name: Self-Sovereign Identity
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Carrying Your Own Identity Wallet
lesson.summary: Self-sovereign identity is the design philosophy that individuals should hold and control their own identity credentials directly, rather than depending on a centralized identity provider for every verification.
lesson.body:
Most identity verification today runs through centralized identity providers: logging in with a big platform account, or a business calling a government database to check a claim. Every use of an identity this way gets logged by that provider, and if the provider goes down, blocks an account, or is compromised, the ability to prove who you are goes down with it. Self-sovereign identity proposes flipping the model: the individual holds their own credentials in a personal digital wallet and presents them directly to whoever needs to verify something, with no intermediary in the loop at the moment of verification.

Self-sovereign identity combines the previous two chapters directly. Decentralized identifiers give the individual an identifier they control cryptographically rather than one a company assigned them, and verifiable credentials give them tamper-evident, digitally signed claims from various issuers, a government, a university, an employer, that they can store and selectively present. A commonly cited set of self-sovereign identity principles includes that individuals should have an independent identity of their own, control over it, access to their own data, and the ability to choose what to disclose and to whom, echoing the selective disclosure idea from the verifiable credential chapter.

A concrete example: the European Union's Digital Identity Wallet initiative is built around this model. A citizen holds a wallet app containing government-issued credentials, an identity document, proof of age, professional qualifications, and presents whichever specific credential, or specific fact drawn from a credential using selective disclosure, a given website or service actually needs, rather than logging in through a company's centralized identity system that tracks every site the citizen visits.

It is worth being honest about the tradeoffs a skeptic should notice. Self-sovereign identity shifts responsibility for safekeeping credentials onto the individual, and losing your keys can mean losing access to everything unless a recovery mechanism exists, which itself reintroduces some trusted party into the picture. It also depends on issuers and verifiers actually adopting compatible standards, a slow, ongoing coordination problem rather than a solved one. Identity Verification still has to happen somewhere. Self-sovereign identity changes who controls the record of that verification and how often it has to be repeated, it does not eliminate the underlying need to establish trust in the first place.
